entry: Organized effort to influence decision-making within a specific group, often an electoral campaign. In democracies, campaigns often aim to choose representatives or decide [[Referendum|referendums]], and the most high-profile ones focus on general [[Election|elections]] and candidates for [[Head of state|head of state]] or [[Head of government|head of government]]. Campaign messages consist of several talking points about policy issues, repeated to make a lasting impression on voters. Most campaigns keep the message broad to attract the most potential voters. In the 2008 American presidential election, [[John McCain]]'s message moved from "Country First" to "The Original Maverick," while [[Barack Obama]] ran on a consistent message of "change." Funding comes from large donors, direct mail to small donors and interest groups, and through Political Action Committees, which the Supreme Court allowed in Citizens United v. FEC (2010). Modern campaigns combine paid staff with volunteers led by campaign managers, political consultants and activists.

Concept in political thought, closely tied to [[Civil liberties|civil liberties]] and [[Human rights|human rights]]. Political freedom has been described as freedom from oppression or coercion, and it is often interpreted negatively as freedom from unreasonable external constraints on action. It can also mean the positive exercise of rights, capacities and possibilities for action. Left-wing philosophy generally couples freedom with positive liberty, the enabling of a group or individual to determine its own life, including freedom from poverty and disease. According to [[Friedrich Hayek]], the "socialist argument" defining individual liberty as "freedom from" obstacles confused the aim of securing individual freedom, because it permitted an identification of freedom with power. [[Milton Friedman]] argued that there cannot be political freedom without economic freedom, while Robin Hahnel took issue with Friedman's concept of economic freedom. [[Michel Foucault]] theorized political freedom in opposition to power relations.

Study of the theoretical and conceptual foundations of politics, also called political theory. It examines the nature, scope and legitimacy of institutions such as [[State (polity)|states]], and the values that guide political action, such as justice, equality and liberty. As a normative field, it focuses on desirable norms, in contrast to political science, which emphasizes empirical description. Major ideologies include [[Anarchism|anarchism]], which rejects the coercive power of centralized governments; [[Conservatism|conservatism]], which seeks to preserve traditional institutions; [[Liberalism|liberalism]], which advocates individual rights and private property; and [[Socialism|socialism]], which emphasizes collective ownership. The field has roots in ancient Greece, where [[Plato]] and [[Aristotle]] discussed justice and ideal states, and in ancient China, where Confucianism, Taoism and legalism emerged.

System for classifying political positions in relation to one another, usually placed along one or more geometric axes. The left–right dimension appears in most long-standing spectra. Its terms derive from seating arrangements in the [[France|French]] parliament after the Revolution (1789–1799), where radicals sat on the left and aristocrats on the right. [[Communism]] and [[Socialism|socialism]] are usually regarded internationally as left, while [[Conservatism|conservatism]] and reactionism are usually regarded as right. [[Liberalism]] can fall on either side. Several political scientists have noted that a single left–right axis is too simplistic, so they add other axes, often splitting economic issues from socio-cultural issues. In 1950 Leonard W. Ferguson factor-analyzed ten attitude scales and identified three factors, which he named religionism, humanitarianism and nationalism.

Powdery substance produced by most types of flowers of seed plants for sexual reproduction. Pollen consists of grains, highly reduced [[Gametophyte|gametophytes]] that produce [[Sperm|sperm]] cells. Each grain has a hard coat of sporopollenin that protects it while it travels from the stamens to the pistil of a flower, or from the male cone to the female cone of a [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperm]]. If pollen lands on a compatible pistil or cone, it germinates and grows a pollen tube that carries sperm to the ovule. The smallest grains, those of forget-me-not, are 2.5–5 μm across, while corn pollen is about 90–100 μm. The study of pollen, palynology, is useful in paleoecology, [[Paleontology|paleontology]], [[Archaeology|archaeology]] and forensics. Pollen is infrequently used as food and is often contaminated by agricultural pesticides.

Transfer of [[Pollen|pollen]] from the anther of a plant to the stigma of a plant, which enables [[Fertilisation|fertilization]] and seed production. Pollinating agents include animals such as [[Bee|bees]], beetles and butterflies, [[Bird|birds]] and [[Bat|bats]], as well as water, wind and plants themselves. Self-pollination can occur within a closed flower, while pollination between species can produce [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] offspring. In angiosperms, the pollen tube carries two gametes to the ovule. One nucleus fuses with polar bodies to form the endosperm, and the other fuses with the [[Egg cell|egg cell]] to form the embryo, a process called double fertilization. In [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]], the ovule is exposed on a support organ such as a cone scale, so penetration of carpel tissue is unnecessary. Christian Konrad Sprengel first addressed pollination as an interaction between flowers and pollen vectors in the 18th century. Because fruiting depends on fertilization, pollination is important in horticulture and agriculture.

Equestrian team sport in which riders use wooden mallets to drive a ball between the opposing team's goal posts. Played on [[Pony|ponyback]], it is one of the oldest known team sports. Outdoor, or field, polo is played on a 300-by-160-yard grass field by two teams of four players, who ride at speeds of up to 35 miles per hour. A game lasts about one and a half to two hours and consists of four to eight seven-minute chukkas, between or during which players change mounts. The progenitor of polo was chovgan, played in Persia ([[Iran]]) and [[Central Asia]] from the 6th century BCE to the 1st century CE, and its modern form developed in India. Polo was patronized by [[Parthian Empire|Parthian]] kings, the [[Sasanian Empire|Sasanian]] court and [[Byzantine Empire|Byzantine]] emperors, and by sultans such as [[Saladin]] and [[Baybars]]. It was an Olympic sport from 1900 to 1936, and it is played professionally in 16 countries.

Rare, highly radioactive metal, sometimes classified as a metalloid, with symbol Po and atomic number 84. It has no stable isotopes, and its natural occurrence is limited to tiny traces of polonium-210, with a half-life of 138 days, in [[Uranium|uranium]] ores. It is chemically similar to [[Selenium|selenium]] and [[Tellurium|tellurium]], although its metallic character resembles that of [[Lead|lead]] and [[Bismuth|bismuth]]. [[Marie Curie|Marie Skłodowska-Curie]] and [[Pierre Curie]] discovered it on August 18, 1898, extracting it from pitchblende and identifying it solely by its strong radioactivity. It was named after Poland, Skłodowska-Curie's homeland. Its applications, all related to its radioactivity, include heaters in space probes, antistatic devices, sources of neutrons and [[Alpha particle|alpha particles]], and poison. It is extremely dangerous to humans.

Transparent thermoplastic, commonly called acrylic or acrylic glass. Synthetic polymer derived from methyl methacrylate, used as an engineering plastic and as a lightweight, shatter-resistant alternative to [[Glass|glass]]. It is also used as a casting resin and in inks and coatings. Trade names include Plexiglas, Perspex and Lucite. The polymer was developed in 1928 by several chemists and first marketed in 1933 by the German firm Röhm & Haas AG as Plexiglas. During [[World War II]], both Allied and Axis forces used acrylic glass for submarine periscopes and aircraft canopies.

Practice of maintaining committed romantic and/or sexual relationships with more than one partner, with the consent of all partners. Many adherents believe in consciously managing [[Jealousy|jealousy]], and polyamorous relationships are loving and intimate rather than purely sexual. The term was coined in 1990 and listed by the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] in 2006. It is considered a queer identity rather than a sexuality or gender identity, and it is not part of the LGBT umbrella but is included in LGBTQ. While mainstream [[Christianity]] and [[Judaism]] generally reject it, [[Hinduism]] and several smaller religions have supported it.

Family of thermoplastic polymers containing carbonate groups. Engineering grades are strong and tough, and they are easily molded and thermoformed. Thermally processed material is usually amorphous and highly transparent, with better light transmission than many kinds of [[Glass|glass]]. Production typically reacts bisphenol A with phosgene, yielding approximately one billion [[Kilogram|kilograms]] of polycarbonate annually. Polycarbonates have no unique resin identification code and are classed as "Other," 7, and products made from them can contain the precursor bisphenol A (BPA).

Paraphyletic class of mostly marine [[Annelid|annelid]] worms, commonly called bristle worms. Each body segment bears a pair of fleshy protrusions called parapodia, which carry many [[Chitin|chitinous]] bristles, or chaetae. More than 10,000 species have been described, living in all of the world's oceans and at all depths, from [[Plankton|planktonic]] species near the surface to a small undescribed species observed at [[Challenger Deep]], the deepest region of the oceans. Many live on [[Abyssal plain|abyssal plains]] and [[Coral reef|coral reefs]], some live [[Parasitism|parasitically]], and a few live in fresh water. Commonly encountered lugworms, bloodworms and sandworms inhabit shallow coasts and are used as fishing bait. Giant tube worms are extremophiles that tolerate near-boiling water near [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]]. Body plans vary widely, reflecting burrowing, swimming and tube-dwelling lifestyles.

[[Hormone|Hormonal]] disorder in women of reproductive age, previously called polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). It is the most common hormonal disorder in this group, occurring in between 5% and 18% of women. Diagnosis requires at least two of three features: irregular menstrual periods, high [[Testosterone|testosterone]] or related symptoms, and an excess of antral ovarian follicles on [[Ultrasound|ultrasound]]. Its cause is uncertain, but there is a clear genetic component. It is linked to insulin resistance, which [[Obesity|obesity]] worsens, raising the risk of type 2 diabetes, liver disease and endometrial cancer. Management includes weight control, hormonal contraception and [[Metformin|metformin]], which increases insulin sensitivity.

Category of [[Polymer|polymers]] containing one or two [[Ester|ester]] linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain. As a specific material, polyester most commonly refers to [[Polyethylene terephthalate|polyethylene terephthalate]] (PET). Natural polyesters occur in plants and insects, including the cutin of plant cuticles and the cellophane-like lining that [[Bee|bees]] of the genus Colletes make for their underground brood cells. Most commercial polyesters are not biodegradable, though natural polyesters and a few synthetic ones are. Polyesters are used extensively in clothing, and [[Cotton|cotton]]-polyester blends can be strong, wrinkle- and tear-resistant, and less prone to shrinking. Polyester [[Fiber|fibers]] have high water, wind and environmental resistance, but they are less fire-resistant and can melt when ignited. Liquid crystalline polyesters, among the first industrially used liquid crystal polymers, are valued for their heat resistance and serve as abradable seals in jet engines.

Most commonly produced [[Plastic|plastic]], a [[Polymer|thermoplastic polymer]] of [[Ethylene|ethylene]] used mainly for packaging, including bags, films, bottles and containers. As of 2017, over 100 million [[Tonne|tonnes]] of polyethylene resin were produced annually, accounting for 34% of the total plastics market. All forms are nontoxic and chemically resilient, which makes polyethylene a long-lived pollutant when disposed of improperly. German chemist Hans von Pechmann first made it by accident in 1898 while investigating diazomethane. Eric Fawcett and Reginald Gibson accidentally produced it again in 1933 at Imperial Chemical Industries (ICI) in England, and by 1935 Michael Perrin had made the process reproducible. During World War II, it was used to insulate coaxial cables in [[Radar|radar]] sets. Milder catalysts followed, beginning with a [[Chromium|chromium]]-based catalyst discovered in 1951 at Phillips Petroleum and a [[Titanium|titanium]]-based system developed by Karl Ziegler in 1953.

Polyether compound derived from [[Petroleum|petroleum]], with applications ranging from industrial manufacturing to [[Medicine|medicine]]. It is also known as polyethylene oxide (PEO) or polyoxyethylene (POE), depending on its molecular weight, and it is commonly incorporated into hydrogels. Pharmaceutical-grade PEG is an excipient in many oral, topical and parenteral products. It is the basis of many laxatives, and its generic laxative name is macrogol. Whole-bowel irrigation with PEG is used for bowel preparation before [[Surgery|surgery]] or colonoscopy. A PEGylated lipid is an excipient in the Moderna and Pfizer–BioNTech vaccines for [[SARS-CoV-2]].

Most common thermoplastic polymer resin of the [[Polyester|polyester]] family. It is used in fibers for clothing, in containers for liquids and food, and in thermoformed manufactured parts, and it is commonly recycled under resin identification code 1. Annual global production reached 31 million tons in 2025, with 2031 projections above 40 million tons. In textiles it is known as polyester, while the acronym PET is generally used for packaging. PET is the fourth most produced polymer, after [[Polyethylene|polyethylene]], [[Polypropylene|polypropylene]] and [[Polyvinyl chloride|polyvinyl chloride]]. More than 60% of PET is produced as polyester fibers.

[[Marriage]] to more than one spouse at the same time. When a man has more than one wife it is called polygyny, and when a woman has more than one husband it is called polyandry. In [[Zoology|zoology]] and sociobiology, the term is used more broadly for any form of multiple mating. In societies that allow it, polygyny is the accepted form in the vast majority of cases. Of 1,231 societies noted in the *Ethnographic Atlas Codebook* from 1960 to 1980, 588 had frequent polygyny, 453 occasional polygyny, 186 were monogamous and 4 had polyandry, though later research found some polyandry in 53 communities. Polygamy is most common in the "polygamy belt" of [[West Africa]] and [[Central Africa]], and its prevalence often correlates with [[Social class|social class]]. In many countries the law recognizes only [[Monogamy|monogamous]] marriages, so polygamy often exists de facto without legal recognition.

Three-dimensional figure with flat polygonal faces, straight edges and sharp corners, or vertices. The term may refer to a solid figure or to its boundary surface. Polyhedra generalize two-dimensional polygons, and convex polyhedra, such as cubes and pyramids, are well defined: each is the convex hull of its vertices. In [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], the volume of a frustum was calculated in the *Moscow Mathematical Papyrus*. [[Platonic solid|Platonic solids]] were studied by ancient Greek mathematicians, and [[Plato]] associated them with the natures of the elements in his *Timaeus*. *Euclid's Elements* treated them later. [[Leonhard Euler]] worked on polyhedral characteristics and on the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem, which underlies the field of [[Topology|topology]]. [[Johannes Kepler]] discovered two non-convex regular polyhedra.

Person whose knowledge spans many different subjects. The word derives from Greek roots meaning "many" and "to learn." Polymaths draw on complex bodies of knowledge to solve specific problems, and some explain their knowledge abstractly and creatively. The concept reflects [[Renaissance]] humanism, which held that humans are limitless in their capacity for development. The term "Renaissance man" describes gifted people of that age who sought to develop their abilities in intellectual, artistic, social, physical and spiritual areas. [[Leonardo da Vinci]] is often described as the archetype of the Renaissance man.

Substance made of very large molecules, or macromolecules, built from many repeating subunits derived from monomers. Polymers are created by polymerization, and their large molecular mass gives them properties such as toughness, high elasticity and a tendency to form amorphous or semicrystalline structures. Natural examples include [[Silk|silk]], wool, amber, hemp, shellac, [[Cellulose|cellulose]] and [[Natural rubber|natural rubber]], and DNA and proteins are biopolymers. Synthetic polymers include [[Polyethylene|polyethylene]], [[Polypropylene|polypropylene]], [[Polystyrene|polystyrene]], polyvinyl chloride, Bakelite and [[Nylon|nylon]]. More than 330 million tons of these synthetic polymers are made every year (2015). The term was coined in 1833 by [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]], but the modern concept of covalently bonded macromolecules was proposed in 1920 by Hermann Staudinger.

Subdiscipline of [[Chemistry|chemistry]] focused on the structures, chemical synthesis, and chemical and physical properties of [[Polymer|polymers]] and macromolecules. Its methods also apply in organic, analytical and physical chemistry, and it typically concerns synthetic and organic compositions such as [[Plastic|plastics]], rubbers and composite materials. In 1834–1844, heating rubber with sulfur was found to greatly improve it, founding the vulcanization process. In 1907 [[Leo Baekeland]] invented [[Bakelite]], the first polymer made independent of the products of organisms. Chemist Hermann Staudinger proposed that polymers consist of long chains of atoms held together by [[Covalent bond|covalent bonds]], which he called macromolecules, and he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1953. Wallace Carothers invented neoprene in 1931 and [[Nylon|nylon]] in 1935.

Laboratory method for rapidly amplifying copies of specific [[DNA]] sequences for detailed study. American biochemist Kary Mullis invented it in 1983 at Cetus Corporation, and he shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with biochemist Michael Smith. The method relies on thermal cycling, which repeatedly heats and cools reagents to separate DNA strands, allow primers to bind, and let [[Enzyme|enzyme]]-driven DNA polymerase assemble new strands from free nucleotides. Almost all applications use a heat-stable enzyme such as Taq polymerase, isolated from the bacterium *Thermus aquaticus*, which survives the high-temperature denaturation step. Before Taq was used, DNA polymerase had to be added manually every cycle. PCR is used in genetic testing and research, in [[DNA profiling|DNA profiling]] for [[Forensic science|forensic science]], and in detecting [[Pathogen|pathogens]] to diagnose infectious diseases.

Mathematical expression built from variables, or indeterminates, and coefficients using only addition, subtraction, multiplication and nonnegative integer exponents. One example in a single variable is x²−4x+7, and an example with three variables is x³+2xyz²−yz+1. Polynomials are used to form equations that encode problems from elementary word problems to complicated scientific ones. Polynomial functions appear in [[Chemistry|chemistry]], [[Physics|physics]], [[Economics|economics]] and [[Social science|social science]], and [[Calculus|calculus]] and [[Numerical analysis|numerical analysis]] use them to approximate other functions. In advanced mathematics, polynomials construct polynomial rings and algebraic varieties, which are central to [[Algebra|algebra]] and [[Algebraic geometry|algebraic geometry]]. The word, first used in the 17th century, combines Greek *poly* ("many") and Latin *nomen* ("name").

Thermoplastic [[Polymer|polymer]] made from the [[Propylene|propylene]] monomer, also known as polypropene. It belongs to the polyolefins and is partially crystalline and nonpolar. It is similar to [[Polyethylene|polyethylene]] but slightly harder and more heat-resistant, and it is a white, mechanically rugged material with high chemical resistance. It is the second most widely produced commodity [[Plastic|plastic]] after polyethylene, and it has the lowest density of the commodity plastics, between 0.895 and 0.93 g/cm³. Its properties depend on molecular weight, crystallinity and isotacticity; isotactic forms are stiffer and more resistant to creep. Phillips Petroleum chemists J. Paul Hogan and Robert Banks first demonstrated the polymerization of propylene in 1951. Giulio Natta and Karl Rehn discovered isotactic polymerization in March 1954, and large-scale commercial production by the Italian firm Montecatini began in 1957.
